decision: Promote the fenced durable JSON mission coordinator onto current mainline as the next lab-grade queue layer, while retaining the in-memory MissionQueue for lightweight local planning.
reviewModel: independent-approach comparison from existing DIG queue experiments plus mainline regression review

evaluatedApproaches.name: current-main-in-memory-queue
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: Good dependency gating and worker capability matching, but process restart loses all mission state and worker ownership.
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: Low for worker crashes or coordinator restarts because state is process-local.
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: Lowest because it is already on main.
evaluatedApproaches.qa: Existing mission queue suite remains part of npm test. Not sufficient for distributed-worker reliability.

evaluatedApproaches.name: worker-id-only durable ownership
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: Insufficient under lease expiry and reclaim because a stale worker identity can write after a new claim generation.
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: Weak under process suspension, delayed messages, and reclaim races.
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: Low implementation complexity but high stale-owner correctness risk.

evaluatedApproaches.name: epoch-plus-uuid-fenced durable JSON store
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: High for a single shared-filesystem coordinator: each claim increments a persistent lease epoch and receives a unique token; heartbeat, complete, and fail require the active worker and current token.
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: Strong against coordinator restart, duplicate claim races, expired owners, and stale completion within the shared-filesystem lab model.
evaluatedApproaches.latency: Higher than in-memory because mutations serialize through an atomic directory lock and whole-state JSON rewrite.
evaluatedApproaches.resourceUse: Low at lab scale; one JSON snapshot plus one lock directory and small lease metadata per mission.
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: Medium: durable callers must propagate leaseToken, but the existing in-memory queue remains unchanged.
evaluatedApproaches.qa: Selected test suite covers persistence, concurrent atomic claim, restart recovery, stale-owner fencing, lease expiry, fenced heartbeat, dependency gating, 12-worker/32-mission contention, clone isolation, malformed inputs, and cancellation.

evaluatedApproaches.name: external transactional coordinator
evaluatedApproaches.correctness: Potentially strongest for real multi-host workers and downstream fencing.
evaluatedApproaches.robustness: Potentially strongest with durable consensus/transaction semantics.
evaluatedApproaches.regressionRisk: High before worker transport and authentication contracts stabilize.
evaluatedApproaches.qa: Deferred until the Qubes transport boundary and authenticated worker protocol are accepted together.

whyItWon: It closes the highest-value reliability gap on current mainline—loss of queued/running missions across restart—without prematurely requiring an external database or network coordinator. It also provides explicit stale-owner fencing while preserving the existing in-memory queue as a low-risk fallback.
changesThisIteration: Rebased the durable coordinator concept onto the current main branch instead of the older experiment branch.
Added deterministic tie-breaking for equal priority/time claims.
Fixed list cloning to avoid passing Array.map callback arguments into structuredClone.
Added explicit cancellation that clears active ownership and fencing state.
Expanded contention coverage from 8 workers/20 missions to 12 workers/32 missions.
Wired durable queue syntax and tests into npm check/test.
failuresAndLessons: A shared-filesystem JSON store is not a distributed database and is not safe evidence for REAL-WORKER READY across separate Qubes domains.
Time-based stale-lock breaking can evict a slow but live lock holder; the real-worker gate needs a stronger process/transport-aware ownership strategy.
Whole-state JSON rewrites are O(n), so throughput and tail latency will degrade with large mission volumes.
Lease fencing protects queue state only; external side effects require idempotency keys or downstream fencing to prevent duplicate effects.
Cancellation currently behaves as an operator override; worker-aware cancellation acknowledgment should be added before remote workers are activated.
Real financial data and transactions remain explicitly out of scope; financial-system testing must remain synthetic and defensive.
realWorkerGates: Run the branch test suite in CI or a local Node environment and record actual pass/fail and duration.
Integrate authenticated worker identity and durable worker sessions with the durable queue lease token.
Exercise crash, process-kill, lock-stall, malformed-store, and power-loss-style fault injection across process boundaries.
Validate qrexec transport behavior in an isolated synthetic Qubes lab with no real financial credentials or transactions.
Add downstream idempotency/fencing contract for any side-effecting worker action.
